---
title: "Detroit Lake Algal Bloom"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
```

USGS operates a continuous water-quality buoy on Detroit Lake, Oregon (site `444306122144600`, `waterservices.usgs.gov/nwis/iv`), reporting hourly. We use two sensor channels:

- `Chlorophyll`: in-situ fluorescence, estimated concentration (ug/L) — total algal biomass, all species
- `Phycocyanin`: in-situ fluorescence at the pigment's specific excitation/emission band (ug/L) — cyanobacteria only, the toxin-producing group

On **2024-07-16** the Oregon Health Authority issued a recreational-use health advisory for Detroit Lake, Big Cliff Reservoir, and the North Santiam River after finding cyanotoxins (microcystin) above safety thresholds — the lake's first cyanobacteria bloom since 2018. We use that date as the start of a documented "bloom" regime; the sensor-recorded phycocyanin signal decays back to pre-bloom levels by late August, so we close the window on 2024-08-24 (we could not confirm an official advisory-lift date for 2024, so this end point is read off the data, not from a press release).

Chlorophyll and phycocyanin are expected to move together during a bloom — cyanobacteria are algae, so a cyanobacteria bloom raises both. Outside a bloom they can diverge: chlorophyll tracks whatever mix of diatoms, green algae, and cyanobacteria happens to be present, while phycocyanin only responds to the cyanobacteria fraction. That's the real relationship the mean shift might be obscuring or, as it turns out here, partly manufacturing.

```{R lake-load}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: lake-load

X_data <- read_csv("../data/real-data/detroit-lake/detroit_lake_2024_season.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(bloom = datetime >= as.POSIXct("2024-07-16", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") &
                 datetime <  as.POSIXct("2024-08-24", tz = "America/Los_Angeles"))

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, c("chl", "pc")])
colnames(X_mat) <- c("Chlorophyll", "Phycocyanin")
win <- 24
```

The record starts 2024-05-16 (a 16-day sensor gap in late April/early May is dropped) and runs through the end of the buoy's 2024 deployment on 2024-11-04, hourly, `r nrow(X_data)` points. Two isolated hourly chlorophyll readings on 2024-10-13 (44.5 and 19.3 ug/L, against a normal range of 0-14) look like a sensor glitch — no matching rise in phycocyanin, no matching event in the record, gone within two hours. We leave them in rather than editing them out; they fall outside the bloom window, so they inflate baseline-group noise rather than distort the bloom signal itself.

```{R lake-oracle}
#| echo: false
#| label: lake-oracle

oracle_resid <- function(X, grp) {
  R <- sapply(colnames(X), function(cn) X[, cn] - ave(X[, cn], grp))
  colnames(R) <- colnames(X)
  R
}

X_oracle <- oracle_resid(X_mat, X_data$bloom)
```

```{R lake-tables}
#| echo: false
#| label: lake-tables

L_ece <- 50

ece_cor <- ece.cor(X_mat, L = L_ece) |> round(3)
rownames(ece_cor) <- colnames(ece_cor) <- colnames(X_mat)

oracle_cor  <- cor(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_cor <- cor(X_mat) |> round(3)

ece_pmat     <- ece_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
oracle_pmat  <- cor_pval(X_oracle) |> round(3)
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_mat) |> round(3)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Plot

```{R fig-lake-series}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Chlorophyll and phycocyanin, Detroit Lake buoy, 2024 season. Teal = documented bloom window (2024-07-16 to 2024-08-24)."
#| fig-height: 6

X_data |>
  select(datetime, bloom, Chlorophyll = chl, Phycocyanin = pc) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Chlorophyll, Phycocyanin), names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(datetime, value, color = bloom)) +
  geom_line(color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_point(size = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~series, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Detroit Lake: Chlorophyll and Phycocyanin, 2024", x = NULL, y = NULL, color = "Bloom") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Phycocyanin sits near zero all season except for a sustained plateau across the bloom window. Chlorophyll spikes at other points too — mid-June, mid-October — that phycocyanin never follows: algal activity that isn't cyanobacteria.

```{R fig-lake-residual}
#| echo: false

X_data |>

  bind_cols(as.data.frame(X_oracle)) |>
  pivot_longer(-datetime, names_to = "series", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(datetime, value, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted") +
```

## ACF

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Oracle

```{R acf-lake-oracle}
#| echo: false

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(2, 3, 2, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 0, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
acf(X_oracle[, "Chlorophyll"], main = "Chlorophyll")
acf(X_oracle[, "Phycocyanin"], main = "Phycocyanin")
mtext("Lag (hours)", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
```

Lag-1 autocorrelation of 0.73 (Chlorophyll) and 0.72 (Phycocyanin) survives bloom-mean removal — hour-to-hour algal biomass has real momentum, same as every other high-frequency sensor chapter in this book.

## Trend

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Oracle

```{R trend-lake-oracle}
#| echo: false

S_oracle <- X_oracle[, "Chlorophyll"] * X_oracle[, "Phycocyanin"]
S_smooth <- stats::filter(S_oracle, rep(1 / win, win), sides = 2)

par(mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
ylim <- quantile(S_oracle, probs = c(0.01, 0.99), na.rm = TRUE)
plot(S_oracle, type = "l", col = "lightgray", ylab = "Chlorophyll x Phycocyanin (oracle residuals)", xlab = "Index (hourly)", ylim = ylim)
abline(h = mean(S_oracle), col = "blue")
lines(S_smooth)
legend("topright", legend = sprintf("%.3f", mean(S_oracle)), text.col = "blue", bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

## Correlation

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_cor,     caption = "ECE Correlation")
knitr::kable(oracle_cor,  caption = "Oracle Correlation")
knitr::kable(pearson_cor, caption = "Pearson Correlation")
```

Naive Pearson finds Chlorophyll-Phycocyanin weakly correlated (0.073) — expected, since most of the record is non-bloom, where the two pigments track different algae. Conditioning on the true bloom window, the oracle correlation jumps to 0.301: within each regime, the two pigments move together far more tightly than the naive number suggests, the opposite of the usual "mean shift inflates naive correlation" story in this book. ECE (`L = 50`) lands at 0.179, between naive and oracle and stable across `L = 20` to `L = 75` (0.159-0.184) — a sensible answer, recovered blind to the 2024-07-16 date.

## P-Values

```{R}
#| layout-ncol: 3
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(ece_pmat,     caption = "ECE P-Values")
knitr::kable(oracle_pmat,  caption = "Oracle P-Values")
knitr::kable(pearson_pmat, caption = "Pearson P-Values")
```

Naive and Oracle both reject independence outright (p < 0.001, n > 4000). ECE does not (p = 0.80). The point estimate is reasonable, but ECE's own moment-based variance is inflated by the lag-1 ≈ 0.73 residual autocorrelation shown above, and that costs it power: a correlation an oracle-informed test finds overwhelming, ECE's blind test can't distinguish from noise.

:::

---

## Bootstrap Methods

```{R}
#| echo: false
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.multiplier")
ece.test(X_mat, type = "bs.parametric")
```

Both bootstrap variants agree with the z-test above: p ≈ 0.58-0.60 (multiplier), p ≈ 0.81-0.83 (parametric) across repeated runs. Neither rejects independence.

## Where this leaves us

Detroit Lake gives ECE a real, dated mechanism (the 2024-07-16 OHA advisory) and a real pair of coupled variables (two algal pigments, one a strict subset of the other's target). The naive-vs-oracle gap runs backwards from most chapters here: the mean shift doesn't inflate naive correlation, it *suppresses* it, because outside the bloom window chlorophyll and phycocyanin are picking up substantially different phytoplankton. ECE's point estimate (0.179) recovers a sensible middle ground between naive (0.073) and oracle (0.301) without ever seeing the advisory date — a genuine win for the moment-based approach.

The p-values tell a less flattering story. Hour-to-hour algal biomass carries real autocorrelation (lag-1 ≈ 0.72-0.73) that survives bloom-mean removal, and it inflates ECE's own variance estimate enough that its bootstrap and z-tests both fail to reject independence, even though naive Pearson and the oracle-informed test both reject at p < 0.001 with the same data. This is the same shape of failure as the interest-rates chapter: a good point estimate paired with a test that autocorrelation has quietly stripped of power.
